title: X OAuth 1.0a access token (oauth_token) next to its secret and the request token that shares its name
summary: The oauth_token value in a signed request's Authorization header, in the access token response and as subject_token in the OAuth 2.0 migration exchange, and the temporary request token that also uses the oauth_token name.
rationale: Claim access-token-in-authorization-header records that the oauth_token value is sent in the clear in every signed request by design; claim signature-derived-from-two-secrets records that only the consumer secret and the token secret are called incredibly sensitive; claim token-exchange-carrier names subject_token as the carrier of the access token in the migration exchange; claim temporary-and-token-credentials-share-names records X's own table in which the request token and the access token both use oauth_token. Whether the access-token half alone is documented as confidential is not stated (open question token-half-sensitivity-still-unsettled), and the request token's lifetime and confidentiality are not stated (request-token-collision-confirmed). No format is stated and the documentation examples differ in shape (examples-not-format). A must-flag for the token half would invent a policy the sources do not support, and a must-not-flag would too. The secret half already has its own Cases. Contract claims cited: oauth1-access-token/access-token-in-authorization-header, oauth1-access-token/signature-derived-from-two-secrets, oauth1-access-token/token-exchange-carrier, oauth1-access-token/temporary-and-token-credentials-share-names.

expectation.rationale: No outcome is asserted for the oauth_token value. Settled by: an X statement about the oauth_token value alone and the request token's lifetime.

sources.supports: X’s implementation requires that requests needing authorization contain an additional HTTP Authorization header with enough information to answer the questions listed above
It is very important to note that these values are incredibly sensitive and should never be shared with anyone.
